newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria shows its people it is hitting corruption.
newsitem.headline: Algeria shows its people it is hitting corruption.

text.p: Algerian authorities have issued a stream of charges and jail sentences on senior officials in state-run companies in a public crackdown on corruption ahead of a referendum to change the constitution.

At least 20 directors or department heads, and traders and accountants, have been charged with embezzlement according to statements, carried on the official Algerian news agency APS, issued by local courts.
Among the directors, one in charge of public works in the northeastern Guelma area has been jailed for eight years. His secretary who was on the run was given a life sentence.

Others in state-run or local authority enterprises include the director of the national electrical household supply branch in the southern Saharan town of Tamanrasset, awaiting trial, the head of a local state medical supplies firm, and two senior officials in different branches of the Local Development Bank.
The government, in the face of apathy and opposition parties' calls for a boycott, is campaigning to try to ensure a high turnout in the November 28 referendum to change the constitution.

The referendum, which strengthens the president's already extensive powers, will ban political parties based on religion, a move the government says will help end five years of violence blamed on Moslem fundamentalist rebels.
Algerian politicians and ordinary citizens have long blamed corruption as a main factor in distrust between the country's 29 million people and the authorities.

Political commentators after general elections in December 1991 said this distrust, and desire for drastic change, were a major factor in the ballot victory of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS). The authorities in January 1992 cancelled the election. Violence erupted shortly afterwards.
